opinions.rationale: The central identification concern is correct: except where consistency links observed outcomes to the strategy, individual counterfactual outcomes are unavailable, and performance measures estimated from observational validation data cannot by themselves test conditional or sequential exchangeability. A held-out sample from the same database addresses overfitting and sampling variability, not unmeasured confounding. Existing work nevertheless supplies identifiable counterfactual calibration, discrimination, and loss measures and shows how predictions can enter decision rules, so neither the validation problem nor the prediction-to-decision mapping is wholly unsolved. Several absolutes are technically wrong. Performance identification in a validation population need not use exactly the assumptions used during model development; it additionally depends on consistency and the relevant treatment, adherence, censoring, and possibly transport conditions. Exchangeability is not empirically testable from the same observed data, but observed treatment support and practical positivity can be diagnosed; structural nonpositivity cannot be repaired by truncation or sensitivity analysis. A randomized rule-versus-usual-care trial identifies the effect of adopting the rule, not the calibration of every individual counterfactual prediction, and it is not the only conceivable causal design. Decisions do not invariably require a scalar threshold, especially for multi-arm or dynamic strategies; they require an explicit action space and utility or loss function. Likewise, a sensitivity parameter for an average treatment effect cannot automatically be carried unchanged into nonlinear calibration, AUC, or Brier-score functionals; a metric-specific sensitivity model must be derived. Simulations can characterize selected confounding scenarios but cannot validate exchangeability in the application. The action-space and causal-validity issues are important for decision-support claims, while extensions to continuous treatments and additional simulation studies are roadmap items rather than universal prerequisites. Literature-novelty assertions such as 'nobody reports' were not judged. No R or Python package capability is asserted here, so no pinned-package source check applies.
opinions.weakest_true_restatement: Counterfactual performance measures for a fixed prediction under a sustained strategy can be identified from observational validation data under explicit consistency, exchangeability, positivity, censoring, and any necessary transport conditions, but those measures do not themselves verify exchangeability. Positivity should be assessed through support diagnostics, with structural violations acknowledged rather than treated as repairable. Some applications also fail to specify the action set and utility or loss function needed to turn counterfactual predictions into a treatment rule; clinical utility then requires evaluation of that explicit policy using a valid causal design.

resolving_work.title: Prediction under interventions: evaluation of counterfactual performance using longitudinal observational data
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides counterfactual calibration, concordance, time-dependent AUC, and Brier-score evaluation for sustained strategies using artificial censoring and weighting, conditional on identification assumptions.

resolving_work.title: Estimating and evaluating counterfactual prediction models
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Provides identification and estimation results for counterfactual loss, ROC-area, and calibration functionals, including evaluation of a fixed misspecified prediction model; it does not verify causal identification assumptions.

resolving_work.title: Aim for clinical utility, not just predictive accuracy
resolving_work.what_it_resolves: Shows that predictions can be mapped into an explicit decision rule and evaluated for clinical utility, refuting the universal claim that nothing maps predictions to decisions while leaving observational identification limitations intact.
